title: Complexe de De Rham à puissance divisée [conférence de 1976 à l’IHÉS] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is a short fragment. The preceding and following folios are unrelated administrative notices, so the context has to come from the cote: notes for a 1976 IHÉS talk on the divided-power de Rham complex.

The page opens mid-sentence: a morphism of the data must 'transform marked section into marked section'. So the objects in play are tuples consisting of:
- a base ring k;
- an object 𝒢 (probably a group- or algebra-like object, or a PD-envelope, over k);
- a distinguished 'marked section'.

From such a tuple a double complex K^{··} is built, presumably a bicomplex mixing a simplicial or Čech-type direction with the divided-power de Rham direction. Morphisms of tuples, required to respect the marked section, induce morphisms of double complexes.

Grothendieck then poses a standard homotopy question. Take two morphisms λ, μ that:
- induce the same morphism on the base, λ_0 = μ_0 : k → k';
- differ on the second component, λ_𝒢, μ_𝒢 : 𝒢 ⇉ 𝒢', both compatible with the marked sections.

What can be said about the induced maps λ, μ : K^{··} → K'^{··}?

The expected answer, in modern terms, is that they are chain-homotopic. This is the usual rigidity or homotopy-invariance property of (PD-)de Rham complexes: two morphisms over the same base map, which agree modulo a divided-power ideal or are linked by a 'difference' of derivation type, induce homotopic maps on de Rham complexes. A canonical homotopy is built from the divided-power Taylor expansion. This is the crystalline mechanism that makes de Rham or crystalline cohomology independent of choices of lifting or embedding.

The page only states the question. No answer or construction appears.

transcription_corrections: 'correspondant à un même [?] homom.': the [?] is a cancelled or underlined stroke after 'même' (triple underline), so the reading is 'correspondant à un même homomorphisme'.
The subscript on the second pair of maps is not clearly 'Φ'. It looks like the same symbol as the object 𝒢 (λ_𝒢, μ_𝒢 : 𝒢 ⇉ 𝒢'), i.e. the components of λ, μ on 𝒢.
'Que peut-on dire [-des-] des hom λ, μ': the struck word is a cancelled 'des'; the question then reads 'des hom λ, μ de K^{··} dans K'^{··}'.
